questions.question: A compiler packs two ALU ops, a load, and a branch into one 128-bit instruction issued every cycle — there is no hardware scheduler; all parallelism was decided at compile time. Which architecture style is this?
questions.explanation: VLIW (Very Long Instruction Word) machines encode several independent operations per instruction slot, relying on the compiler — not dynamic hardware — to expose parallelism.

questions.question: A short if/else compiles with no branch at all: both the 'then' and 'else' instructions are emitted, each tagged with a condition flag, and only the instructions whose flag is true commit. What are such instructions called?
questions.explanation: Predication attaches a condition (predicate) to each instruction so both paths execute but only the matching side retires, converting control flow into data flow and removing branches.

questions.question: On SPARC, a procedure call needs no register saves: the callee automatically sees a fresh register set that shares a few slots with the caller's, which carry the passed arguments. What is this mechanism?
questions.explanation: SPARC's register windows rotate on call/return so each procedure gets its own registers; the overlap region (outs of caller = ins of callee) passes arguments without memory traffic.

questions.question: On Intel Itanium, the compiler — not the hardware — finds parallelism and groups three operations per bundle, with a template field declaring which can issue together. What is this design philosophy?
questions.explanation: EPIC (Explicitly Parallel Instruction Computing), used in IA-64/Itanium, pushes ILP discovery into the compiler; bundles and template bits tell the hardware which operations issue in parallel.

questions.question: In classic MIPS assembly, the instruction written directly after a 'beq' executes even when the branch is taken — compilers fill the position with useful work rather than let it bubble. What is this position called?
questions.explanation: Because the branch's effect is pipelined, the instruction after it has already been fetched and always executes — the branch delay slot, which good compilers fill with an independent instruction.

questions.question: A decoder sees CMP R1, R2 immediately followed by BEQ and merges the pair into a single fused micro-op, freeing an issue slot in the back end. What is this optimization called?
questions.explanation: Macro-op (instruction) fusion lets the decoder merge a compare plus a dependent branch into one uop, effectively executing two instructions for the cost of one slot.

questions.question: A CPU must execute 'shift left by N' where N arrives in a register at runtime, and every possible shift — 1 to 31 bits — must complete in a single cycle. Which hardware block, built from a matrix of multiplexers, does this?
questions.explanation: A barrel shifter uses log2(n) stages of 2:1 multiplexers so any rotate/shift amount resolves combinationally in one cycle, unlike an iterative serial shifter.

questions.question: A GPU executes one instruction stream in which the 32 threads of a warp run it in lockstep on their own data, diverging at branches and reconverging afterward. What is this execution model called?
questions.explanation: Single Instruction, Multiple Threads is NVIDIA's model: scalar-looking code runs across a warp of threads with hardware-managed divergence — distinct from classic SIMD lanes.

questions.question: Firmware for a memory-constrained smartwatch shrinks by 30% when rebuilt so common instructions encode in 16 bits instead of 32, like ARM's Thumb or RISC-V's C extension. What is this ISA feature called?
questions.explanation: Compressed instruction sets (ARM Thumb/Thumb-2, RISC-V 'C') offer short encodings for frequent instructions, improving code density and I-cache efficiency at some encoding-space cost.

questions.question: A shared library's branch and data references are encoded as offsets added to the current program counter rather than absolute addresses, so the code runs correctly at whatever base it is loaded. Which addressing mode enables this?
questions.explanation: PC-relative (x86-64 calls it RIP-relative) addressing computes the target as PC + displacement, the foundation of position-independent code that needs no relocation at load time.

questions.question: In indexed addressing, if the base register contains 2000 and the index register contains 250, what is the effective address?
questions.explanation: The effective address is base plus index: 2000 + 250 = 2250.

questions.question: The instruction LOAD R1, 40(R2) uses which addressing mode?
questions.explanation: The notation 40(R2) adds displacement 40 to the base register R2 to compute the effective address, which is base-displacement (indexed) addressing.

questions.question: How many memory accesses are required to fetch an operand using memory indirect addressing?
questions.explanation: Memory indirect addressing requires one access to read the pointer word and a second access to fetch the actual operand.

questions.question: If an instruction format reserves 7 bits for the opcode field, how many distinct operations can be encoded?
questions.explanation: A 7-bit opcode field encodes 2^7 = 128 distinct operation codes.

questions.question: The x86 instruction MOV EAX, [EBX + 4*ECX + 16] uses which addressing mode?
alternatives: Base plus scaled index plus displacement
questions.explanation: The effective address combines a base register, an index register scaled by 4, and a displacement — the scaled indexed (SIB) mode.

questions.question: Execute this sequence: R1 <- 5; ADD R1, R1, R1; SUB R1, R1, #7. What is the final value of R1?
questions.explanation: ADD doubles R1 to 10, then SUB subtracts the immediate 7, leaving 3.

questions.question: For LDR R1, [R2, #16] with R2 = 0x2000, what effective memory address is accessed?
questions.explanation: The effective address is base register plus displacement: 0x2000 + 0x10 = 0x2010.

questions.question: In ADD R1, R2, #5, the operand value 5 is encoded directly inside the instruction word. What addressing mode is used for that operand?
questions.explanation: Immediate addressing embeds the operand itself in the instruction, needing no register or memory read.

questions.question: An ISA defines 64 distinct opcodes and 32 general-purpose registers. How many bits are required for the opcode field and for each register field, respectively?
questions.explanation: log2(64) = 6 bits for the opcode; log2(32) = 5 bits to name each register.

questions.question: A fixed-length 32-bit instruction uses 6 bits for the opcode and two 5-bit register fields. How many bits remain for the immediate field?
questions.explanation: 32 - 6 - 5 - 5 = 16 bits, as in the MIPS I-type format.
